rows.grounds: sinking into body and other objects

items.question: What happens to those who do not become inwardly identified with that sound?
premises: Inner identity with one's own kind is perceived instantly.
Some do not attain absorption in that sound.
Without that absorption they sink into the body and other objects.
items.inference: Failure to become inwardly absorbed in the sound results in immersion in bodily and external identification.
uncertainties: The bracketed reading sājātyāntarma[ttama]yībhūtir is slightly unclear in the supplied text.
items.plain_english: For those in whom inner identity with that sound is instantly recognized, absorption occurs; but those who do not become absorbed in it sink into identification with the body and other things.

rows.grounds: taking consciousness as sunk while missing the heart
sounds from drums and similar sources

items.question: How should the sound arising from instruments like drums be understood in this context?
premises: Some people do not recognize the heart and take consciousness as merely submerged.
Sounds arise from sources such as skin-covered instruments.
Such a sound is the dhvani being discussed here.
items.inference: The sound produced by instruments like drums is the relevant dhvani, though it may be misunderstood by those who miss the heart.
uncertainties: The exact syntactic break in magnasaṃvinmānāstvahṛdayā is compressed and could be parsed in more than one way.
items.plain_english: Those who do not know the heart think consciousness is merely submerged; in that context, the sound that arises from things like skin-covered drums is the dhvani being referred to.

the quality of being tinged or resonant

items.question: Why is this sound described as madhyamā and associated with a coloring quality?
premises: The sound is both clear and unclear in form.
It appears in a gross aspect.
Within madhyamā an undivided element is still present.
items.inference: Because it mixes distinctness with indistinctness and retains an undivided element, the sound is madhyamā and has a coloring quality.
uncertainties: raktatā can suggest redness or affective coloring; the verse supports the latter but does not make it explicit.
items.plain_english: That sound is called madhyamā because it is partly clear and partly unclear and appears in a gross form; since an undivided element remains within it, it has a coloring or resonant quality.

rows.gloss: it may be that is delighting

rows.grounds: from the practice of tala and recitation

items.question: Why does an undivided sonic nature produce delight and fulfillment?
premises: Where the nature is undivided, it becomes delighting.
Undividedness conduces to fulfillment.
This can be observed in rhythmic recitation.
items.inference: Undivided sonic nature delights because undividedness itself brings fulfillment, as seen in rhythmic recitation.
uncertainties: tālapāṭhataḥ may refer specifically to musical meter, recitative rhythm, or both.
items.plain_english: When the sound is of an undivided nature, it becomes pleasing; for undividedness brings fulfillment, as can be seen in rhythmic recitation.

items.question: What level of speech is indicated as the cause behind the arising of distinct phonemes?
premises: People feel satisfaction in an unmanifest sound during musical playing.
Distinct phonemes arise later as articulated forms.
There must be a causal level prior to the arising of distinct phonemes.
items.inference: The satisfying unmanifest sound points to a prior causal level of speech underlying the emergence of distinct phonemes.
uncertainties: The verse implies but does not explicitly name the causal level as paśyantī or madhyamā.
items.plain_english: One feels satisfied in that unmanifest sound during musical playing; but the power that serves as the cause for the arising of distinct phonemes is a deeper level than that articulation.

rows.grounds: the reflective linkage analogous to the initial one

items.question: What characterizes vaikharī speech within the gross triad described here?
premises: Vaikharī is the gross level of speech.
Its function is mainly sentences and other articulated discourse.
Within the gross triad there is a connecting awareness analogous to the first.
items.inference: Vaikharī is the gross, outwardly articulated level whose main function is discourse, yet it still contains a reflective linkage within the gross triad.
uncertainties: The phrase anusandhānamādivat is terse and its exact referent within the triad is not fully explicit.
items.plain_english: That gross level is vaikharī, whose main function is sentences and other spoken forms; and within this gross triad there is still a connecting awareness like the first.

rows.grounds: the same three considered one by one
is designated as the subtle level

items.question: How is the subtle level distinguished from the gross level in this triad?
premises: The same triad can be considered separately.
When considered separately it is called subtle.
Examples include intending to produce ṣaḍja, to play sweetly, and to speak words.
items.inference: The subtle level is the triad experienced as distinct intentional acts prior to their fused gross expression.
uncertainties: The mapping of the three examples to the three members of the triad is implied rather than stated explicitly.
items.plain_english: When that same triad is taken separately, it is called subtle, as in the distinct intentions: I make the ṣaḍja, I play sweetly, I speak words.

rows.grounds: the initial member of this threefold set

items.question: What is the highest aspect within the subtle triad of reflective awareness?
premises: The threefold connecting awareness is experienced separately.
This triad itself has a first member.
That first member is without limiting conditions.
items.inference: Within the subtle triad, the highest aspect is the first reflective awareness, which is free of limiting adjuncts.
uncertainties: The verse identifies the first member as anupādhimat but does not name it with a technical speech-level term.
items.plain_english: The threefold connecting awareness is indeed experienced separately; and of this triad too, the first aspect is the one whose form is free of limiting conditions.

rows.grounds: three principal powers in this context

items.question: What is the supreme triad and what powers operate within it?
premises: There is a supreme triad beyond the conditioned levels.
In that triad Śiva is of the nature of supreme consciousness.
For the appearing of division, three principal powers are present.
items.inference: The supreme triad is Śiva as supreme consciousness together with three principal powers through which division appears.
uncertainties: The supplied token mukhyāstisro@tra contains an editorial marker that may reflect a sandhi or source issue.
items.plain_english: That supreme triad is Śiva, whose nature is supreme consciousness; and for the appearing of division, three principal powers are present there.

rows.grounds: the power of opening known as jñāna

items.question: Which three principal powers are identified in the supreme triad?
premises: The supreme triad contains three principal powers.
One is anuttarā, another is supreme will.
The unfolding power called knowledge is taught as the lower of these three.
items.inference: The three principal powers are anuttarā, supreme will, and the unfolding knowledge-power designated as aparā.
uncertainties: The verse names the third as jñānākhyā/aparā but compresses its relation to parāparā into a brief phrase.
items.plain_english: The three principal powers are anuttarā, supreme will, and the unfolding power called knowledge, which is declared as the lower one.

rows.gloss: again from their stirring are declared
from entry as the expressed power of action

items.question: How do the three principal powers expand into six pure cognitions?
premises: The three powers undergo stirring.
From that stirring six immaculate cognitions are declared.
This occurs through their entry functioning as the power of action.
items.inference: The stirring of the three principal powers, as they enter into action, unfolds them into six pure cognitions.
uncertainties: The token saṃvido@malāḥ contains an editorial marker; the intended reading is taken as saṃvido'malāḥ.
items.plain_english: From the stirring of those powers, six immaculate cognitions are declared; this happens through their entry as the expressed power of action.

rows.gloss: this much of the God of gods
rows.grounds: to this extent belonging to the supreme deity

items.question: What is the significance of the twelve cognitions in the deity's power-wheel?
premises: Twelve cognitions are declared.
In these twelve the whole is completed.
This constitutes the principal power-wheel of the God of gods.
items.inference: The twelve cognitions form the primary wheel of powers in which the entirety of manifestation is comprehensively contained.
items.plain_english: Twelve cognitions are taught, and in them everything is completed; this is the principal wheel of powers of the God of gods.

rows.gloss: by being of the nature of reflective awareness

rows.grounds: by the conjunction of projection and retraction

items.question: How is Bhairava described as fully empowered in this phase of emanation?
premises: By this extent the God of gods is full of power.
He is Bhairava.
His nature is reflective awareness operating through emission and withdrawal.
items.inference: Bhairava is fully empowered as reflective awareness that manifests through the twin movements of emission and withdrawal.
items.plain_english: To this extent the God of gods, Bhairava, is full of power; his nature is reflective awareness, operating through emission and withdrawal.

items.question: Why are these powers called Kālikās and how are they presented in the Sāraśāstra?
premises: These powers are known through the cognition of determinate measure.
In some sources they are called Kālikās.
The Sāraśāstra speaks of worshiping the supreme one-syllabled power at the center.
items.inference: Because they are apprehended as determinate measures of manifestation, these powers are called Kālikās, and the Sāraśāstra centers them in the supreme one-syllabled reality.
uncertainties: The exact doctrinal reason for the name Kālikā is only suggested here through iyattākalanā.
items.plain_english: Because they are known through a determinate measuring, these powers are in some places called Kālikās; and the Sāraśāstra also speaks of the supreme one-syllabled power at the center.

rows.gloss: one should worship the one called Bhairava-self
rows.grounds: worship the supreme identified as the self of Bhairava

items.question: How does the power-wheel expand from the central Bhairava reality?
premises: The Bhairava-self is to be worshiped at the center.
It is surrounded by twelve yoginīs.
From these the wheel of powers extends up to sixty-four.
items.inference: The central Bhairava reality unfolds outward as a wheel of powers, first as twelve yoginīs and then expanding to sixty-four.
uncertainties: The form tābhya is irregular in the supplied text and is read contextually as ablative plural.
items.plain_english: One should worship the Bhairava-self surrounded by twelve yoginīs; from them the wheel of powers extends up to sixty-four.

items.question: How far does the expansion of the powers extend and why do their names vary?
premises: The unfolding proceeds from ekāra onward.
It extends up to a thousand-spoked form.
The powers receive many names in scripture according to their functions.
items.inference: The power-wheel expands vastly from ekāra to a thousandfold form, and its many names reflect differences in function taught in the scriptures.
uncertainties: sahasrāraṃ may be literal, symbolic, or both; the verse does not specify.
items.plain_english: Beginning from the syllable e, the unfolding proceeds up to a thousand-spoked wheel; and in the scriptures these powers are given many names according to their different functions.

rows.gloss: through dual, nondual, and mixed forms
rows.grounds: by conjunction of dualistic, nondualistic, and blended approaches

items.question: How are the modes of worship of these powers classified in the Traiśira?
premises: The powers have associated modes of worship.
These modes take dual, nondual, and mixed forms.
The Traiśira explains this at great length.
items.inference: The worship of these powers is classified into dual, nondual, and mixed approaches, as elaborated extensively in the Traiśira.
items.plain_english: Their modes of worship take dual, nondual, and mixed forms, and this is explained at great length in the revered Traiśira.

rows.gloss: from fear of prolixity and from lack of use

items.question: Why does the text not elaborate the Traiśira teaching here, and how are the powers described?
premises: The Traiśira teaching is extensive.
The author avoids prolixity and unnecessary repetition here.
The same powers are proclaimed as stainless, pure, and aghora.
items.inference: The author omits the lengthy Traiśira exposition here for brevity and relevance, while affirming that these powers are stainless, pure, and aghora.
items.plain_english: This is not written out here for fear of making the work too long and because it is not needed; those same powers are proclaimed as stainless, pure, and aghora.

items.question: How can the pure aghora powers also be related to the terrible powers and the cosmic functions?
premises: There are terrible and more terrible powers.
The aghora powers are their source.
The same powers operate in creation, maintenance, dissolution, and beyond those three conditions.
items.inference: Because they are the source of the terrible powers, the aghora powers are essentially related to them and pervade creation, maintenance, dissolution, and the transcendence of that triad.
uncertainties: The verse compresses the relation between sourcehood and identity; the exact ontological nuance is brief.
items.plain_english: Because they are the source of the terrible and more terrible powers, those same aghora powers are of that nature too; they operate in creation, maintenance, and dissolution, and also in the transcendence of those three conditions.

items.question: How do the teachers classify the form of these powers beyond limiting conditions?
premises: The abiding form of these powers is divided in many ways.
There is a form beyond limiting conditions.
The teachers declare that transcendent form to be twofold.
items.inference: Although the powers appear in many divisions, their form beyond limiting conditions is taught by the masters as twofold.
items.plain_english: The abiding form of those same powers is divided in many ways; but the form beyond limiting conditions, the teachers say, is twofold.

rows.gloss: from the non-arising of limiting conditions
by the method of forceful ripening
rows.grounds: through the process of intense maturation

items.question: What are the two ways the transcendent state beyond limiting conditions is attained?
premises: The transcendent state may occur because limiting conditions do not arise.
Or it may occur through pacification of limiting conditions.
Pacification itself is twofold: by quieting and by forceful ripening.
items.inference: The state beyond limiting conditions is reached either by their non-arising or by their pacification, and pacification occurs either gently or through forceful ripening.
uncertainties: haṭhapāka is a technical expression; the verse supports 'forceful ripening' but not a more specific ritual or yogic method.
items.plain_english: That transcendent state comes either because limiting conditions do not arise, or because they are pacified; and pacification is twofold, by quiet settling or by the method of forceful ripening.

rows.gloss: by what is called the savor of devouring
rows.grounds: by the relish known as total assimilation
the calming that comes through intense maturation

items.question: Why is the third mode of pacification especially suited for instruction?
premises: There is a blazing, continual savor of devouring.
Through it occurs pacification by forceful ripening.
This mode burns up the fuel of difference.
items.inference: The third mode, forceful ripening through the blazing savor of devouring, is especially suited for instruction because it directly burns away the fuel of difference.
uncertainties: The verse calls it the third, while the previous verse described pacification as twofold; the numbering may reflect a broader classification.
items.plain_english: The pacification that comes through forceful ripening, as a continual blazing savor of devouring, is especially fit for instruction, because it burns up the fuel of difference.

rows.gloss: in the belly-fire of one's own awareness
rows.grounds: in the inner fire of innate knowing

items.question: What happens when all states are forcefully offered into the fire of one's own awareness?
premises: All states are forcefully offered into the belly-fire of one's own awareness.
By their own power they kindle that fire.
As a result they abandon differentiated division.
items.inference: When all states are forcefully offered into innate awareness, they fuel that fire and lose their divided, differentiated character.
items.plain_english: When all states are forcefully offered into the fire of one's own awareness, they kindle that fire by their own power and abandon the divisions of difference.

rows.gloss: they consume what has become nectar
rows.grounds: they partake of the immortal essence

items.question: What do the goddesses of consciousness consume when differentiated forms are dissolved by forceful ripening?
premises: Forceful ripening dissolves the divided forms of states.
When those forms are melted away, what remains becomes nectar.
The goddesses of consciousness consume that nectar-like universe.
items.inference: Through forceful ripening, differentiated forms dissolve into nectar, and the goddesses of consciousness consume the universe in that immortal essence.
items.plain_english: When, through forceful ripening, the divided forms of all states are dissolved, the goddesses of consciousness consume the universe as it becomes nectar.
